summary.text: The binomial distribution gives the probability of each possible number of successes in n independent yes-no experiments, each with success probability p.
A single success-or-failure experiment is a Bernoulli trial, and with just one trial the binomial distribution becomes a Bernoulli distribution.
It models successes in a sample drawn with replacement; without replacement the draws are not independent and the result is hypergeometric instead.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: The number of trials n and the success probability p

facts.label: One trial
facts.value: With n = 1 it is a Bernoulli distribution

facts.label: Same-probability sequences
facts.value: Any sequence with k successes is equally probable, wherever they fall

facts.label: Large populations
facts.value: Stays a good approximation when N is much larger than n

facts.label: Used in testing
facts.value: It is the basis for the binomial test of significance

items.prompt: Three independent shots each have the same chance of going in. Sequence one: in, in, miss. Sequence two: miss, in, in. How do their probabilities compare?

options.label: They are equal
Sequence one is likelier, since it starts well
Sequence two is likelier, since it ends well

items.explain: With independent trials and a constant chance, any sequence with the same number of successes is equally probable, wherever they fall.

items.prompt: You take 4 independent shots and score exactly once. In how many different orders could that one success have come?
items.explain: Counting the sequences means choosing which trial holds the success. With 4 trials there are 4 places for it.

options.label: Marbles have more than two colours
Three draws is too few for any distribution
Each draw is a certain success

items.explain: Sampling without replacement makes the draws dependent, so the result is hypergeometric rather than binomial.

items.prompt: A pollster picks 100 people from a country of millions, never asking anyone twice, and counts the yes answers. Is the binomial distribution reasonable?

options.label: No, because picking without replacement rules it out
Yes, as a good approximation, since the population is far larger than the sample
Yes, but only if the pollster picks the same person twice
No, because the answers must be exactly independent

items.explain: Without replacement the draws are not independent, but when the population is much larger than the sample the binomial remains a good approximation.

items.prompt: You run one yes-no experiment and count its successes, which can only be 0 or 1. Which distribution is the binomial in this case?

options.label: Hypergeometric
Bernoulli
A distribution with n = 0
Binomial with no parameters

items.explain: With a single trial (n = 1) the binomial distribution is a Bernoulli distribution.

paragraphs.heading: Counting successes
paragraphs.text: Picture running the same yes-or-no experiment n times in a row. Each try is independent of the others, and each one comes out as a success with probability p or a failure with probability q = 1 − p. The binomial distribution tells you how likely each possible number of successes is across all n tries. If a random variable X behaves this way, we write X ~ B(n, p), where n is a natural number and p lies between 0 and 1.

paragraphs.heading: Built from Bernoulli trials
paragraphs.text: A single experiment that can only succeed or fail goes by the name Bernoulli trial, and a run of such outcomes is called a Bernoulli process. So the binomial distribution is really about a string of Bernoulli trials. With only one trial, when n = 1, it reduces to what is called the Bernoulli distribution. It also serves as the foundation of the binomial test, a tool for judging statistical significance.

paragraphs.heading: Where the formula comes from
paragraphs.text: Take one particular string of n trials holding k successes and n − k failures. The chance of seeing exactly that string is pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ. Since the trials are independent and the chances stay fixed from one trial to the next, every such string has this same probability, wherever the successes happen to sit. Printed tables of binomial probabilities usually only run up to n/2, because for k > n/2 you can get the value from its complement, since f(k; n, p) matches f(n − k; n, 1 − p).

paragraphs.heading: The typical outcome
paragraphs.text: For X ~ B(n, p), the expected value is E [X] = np, the number of trials times the chance of success on each. If np happens to be an integer, the mean, the median and the mode all land on that same value, np. With p = 0, getting zero successes is certain, and with p = 1, all n trials succeed, so the mode is 0 in the first case and n in the second.

paragraphs.heading: Estimating p from data
paragraphs.text: When the number of trials n is known, p can be estimated by the fraction of trials that succeeded, p̂ = x/n. Two standard routes give this same answer: maximum likelihood estimation and the method of moments. The estimate is unbiased and has minimum variance. For large samples it is approximately normal, thanks to the central limit theorem, since it amounts to averaging Bernoulli samples.

paragraphs.heading: With or without replacement
paragraphs.text: A common use is counting successes in a sample of size n taken with replacement from a population of size N. If the items are not put back, the draws stop being independent, and the count follows a hypergeometric distribution rather than a binomial one. Even so, when N is far bigger than n, the binomial still approximates the answer well, and it is widely used.
